extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in Stoic philosophy (undergraduate/graduate students, self-learners, and philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: An overview/introduction to Stoic philosophy covering its history, major figures, and its three-part structure (physics, logic, ethics), with emphasis on doctrine and practical application. Intended to present core Stoic concepts and how they interrelate for readers learning or teaching Stoicism.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Three Parts of Stoic Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy is organically divided into three interconnected parts: physics, logic, and ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physics tells what the world is and how it formed; logic organizes discourse and defends against sophistries; ethics shows the appropriate action for each case and how to harmonize with individual and universal nature. The three are compared to an orchard (fence = logic; trees = physics; fruits = ethics) and to parts of an animal (bones/tendons = logic; flesh = physics; soul = ethics). Emphasize interdependence: do not treat the parts in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic Physics (including Logos, Providence, and Primordial Fire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic physics posits a corporeal Universal Intelligence (Logos) identified with a demiurgic/primordial fire that is also Providence and fate; the world is produced and governed by this Logos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain Logos as Universal Intelligence/Divinity (pyr) that provides beings with what they need (paraskeue), governs causally (heimarmene), and shapes the cosmos. Discuss providential but limited nature of Divine calculation (imperfections and unpredictability exist). Present the cosmological cycles (fire→air→water→earth and back) and the concept of ekpyrosis (conflagration and rebirth). Connect physics to ethical conclusions (e.g., follow Nature as cosmic order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic Ontology: Pneuma and Hyle (elements and transformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: All beings are a combination of pneumatic substance (pneuma) and inert matter (hyle); the four phenomenological elements (fire, air, water, earth) transform cyclically into one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how fire and air (active) form pneuma, water and earth (passive) form hyle, and how balance between expansion and contraction grants reality to beings. Include the cyclical transformations (fire→air→water→earth and reverse). Use this framework to explain persistence, change, and dissolution of beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four Degrees of Tonicity of the Pneuma
rubrics_metrics.description: The pneuma manifests in four degrees of tonicity corresponding to types of beings: (1) physical structure of inanimate beings (hexis), (2) nature of plants (physis), (3) soul of animals (psyche), (4) rational human soul (hegemonikon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain tonicity as density/tension: lower tonicity = denser, less tensioned (inanimate); higher tonicity = more tensioned, less dense (rational soul). Associate functions: unification (hexis), growth (physis), representation and impulse (psyche), and rational interpretation, assent, and guidance (hegemonikon). Use Chrysippus' examples and the table of degrees as teaching tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational Soul and Human Capacity for Assent
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans possess a rational soul (hegemonikon) that uniquely has the power of assent (synkatathesis), enabling non-automatic reactions to representations and thereby moral responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize distinction between animals (impulses determined by perceptions) and humans (control over assent and impulses). Use examples (fear of dogs depends on opinion) and Chrysippus' cylinder analogy to illustrate how nature shapes responses but assent mediates action. Connect this capacity to ethical agency and Stoic rehabilitation of freedom within causal determinism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciling Determinism and Human Freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism reconciles cosmic determinism (causal chains initiated by the Demiurge) with human freedom by locating moral choice in the power to assent and in acting within one's sphere of influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain humans as co-artisans of destiny: although causal chains constrain events, individuals determine reactions and thereby contribute to cosmic administration. Discuss limits on Providence (matter resists pneuma; Divine foresight limited) and how moral responsibility functions within these limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics: Following Nature and Appropriate Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics instructs what action is appropriate in each case and how to harmonize with one's individual nature and with Nature as a whole; the Stoic motto is to 'follow Nature'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify that 'follow Nature' refers both to the Nature of the world (cosmic pneuma) and to each individual's own nature. Ethics is practical and action-guiding. Prepare to connect ethical precepts to Stoic physics (what nature is) and to logic (how to form correct judgments). Note that interpretations vary and will be examined in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic in Stoicism (scope and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic logic covers more than modern formal logic: it includes theory of knowledge, theory of language, propositional logic, the study of sophisms, rhetoric, and tools for defending against false appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach logic both as formal argumentation (validity, true premises) and as practical skill to detect sophistries and shape discourse. Include discussion of phantasia (representations) and the Stoic concern with producing cogent demonstrations and avoiding false arguments that seem true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phantasia (Representation) and its Role in Epistemology
rubrics_metrics.description: Phantasia designates the concrete content apprehended by senses, imagination, memory, or thought; in Chrysippus it has two facets: a sensible modification and a virtual linguistic form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss translation issues (appearance, impression, representation) and explain how phantasia links perception to assent and action. Emphasize its centrality for logical, epistemological, and ethical issues: correct phantasia and proper assent underpin right action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as a Way of Life / Practical Vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism aims to create an inner discourse to replace unreflective common sense; it is a practical art of living involving self-examination, continuous questioning, and application of doctrines to daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight historical examples (Socrates, Epictetus, Seneca, Musonius Rufus) and practices (self-correction: 'remove some of my vices daily'). Warn against reducing Stoicism to mottos; instead teach methods for dialogical examination, dialectical debate, and moral practice. Stress that Stoic knowledge is dialogical and subject to internal debate and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of Judgment (Epistemic Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence is lacking, one must suspend assent rather than give it or deny; skeptics extend this but Stoics apply suspension where appropriate (e.g., 'The number of stars is odd').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat suspension as a methodological rule in epistemology: do not assent when there is no evidence either way. Use it to contrast Stoic positions with radical skepticism and to ground cautious deliberation in ethics and logic.
